::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Let $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = \sin{\frac{1}{x}}$. Then f is not uniformly continuous](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1692053/let-f-mathbbr-0-to-mathbbr-fx-sin-frac1x-then-f-is-not), asked by [L.F. Cavenaghi](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/248387/l-f-cavenaghi) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-03-10; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I am not sure if I know what I have to do. I imagine that supposing that the opposite I should get any contradiction, but, how to choose $\epsilon$ and $x$, $y$, for this?
>
> Thanks!
:::

The definition of uniformly continuous is:

> **For every** $\epsilon > 0$ **there exists** a $\delta > 0$ such that **for all** $x$ and $y$, $|x-y| < \delta \implies$|f(x) - f(y)| < \epsilon$.

To negate the definition you have to bubble the “not” down through all the quantifiers and the implication:

> **There exists** an $\epsilon > 0$such that **for every**$\delta > 0$**there exist** numbers$x$and$y$such that$|x-y| < \delta$but$|f(x) - f(y)| \geq \epsilon$.

If you look at the graph of this function (or a computer's best approximation to the graph), you'll see that the values 1 and -1 are achieved infinitely often in every interval containing the origin.
